steps.title: Useful words and phrases
steps.intro: In this unit you will learn about: greetings and introductions · a fi (to be) and other useful verbs · numbers up to a hundred · positive and negative forms.

steps.title: Dialogue 1 — La hotel
steps.context: Mike Foster, a businessman from Scotland, has recently arrived in Bucharest and is looking for a place to sit down in his hotel lobby. He sees an empty seat next to a young woman.

lines.speaker: Mike
lines.ro: Bună dimineața, domnișoară. E liber aici, vă rog?
lines.en: Good morning, miss. Is this seat free, please?

lines.speaker: Domnișoară
lines.en: Yes. Please, go ahead and sit down.

lines.speaker: Mike
lines.en: Thank you. Are you staying in the hotel?

lines.speaker: Domnișoară
lines.en: Yes, I am staying here.

lines.speaker: Mike
lines.en: Are you from Romania?

lines.speaker: Domnișoară
lines.ro: Da, sunt româncă. Sunt din Timișoara. Dar dumneavoastră?
lines.en: Yes, I am Romanian. I am from Timișoara. And you?

lines.speaker: Mike
lines.ro: Eu sunt din Marea Britanie, din Edinburgh. Sunt scoțian. Și cât timp stați în București?
lines.en: I am from Britain, from Edinburgh. I am Scottish. And how long are you staying in Bucharest?

lines.speaker: Domnișoară
lines.ro: Stau numai patru zile. Dar dumneavoastră?
lines.en: I am only staying four days. And you?

lines.speaker: Mike
lines.ro: Eu stau trei luni. Sunt om de afaceri. Mă numesc Mike Foster. Și dvs?
lines.en: I am staying three months. I am a businessman. My name is Mike Foster. What is yours?

lines.speaker: Domnișoară
lines.ro: Eu sunt Rodica Mihai, sunt ziaristă la ziarul 'Azi'.
lines.en: Rodica Mihai. I am a journalist on the newspaper 'Today'.

lines.speaker: Mike
lines.en: Is what you do interesting?

lines.speaker: Domnișoară
lines.ro: În general, da. Vorbiți limba română?
lines.en: In general, yes. Do you speak Romanian?

lines.speaker: Mike
lines.en: Unfortunately, not very well.

steps.title: Introducing yourself
steps.explanation: When you ask a stranger a question or request help, use the following gambit:
steps.callout: Notice in the dialogue how Mike says vă rog, domnișoară when he asks if he can sit down and the young lady uses poftiți in reply. Poftiți in this situation means 'please, go ahead'. Using the dialogue as a guide, try: asking someone if they are from Romania; asking someone if they are from Britain; asking a man if he is Scottish; asking a young lady if she is Romanian.

steps.title: Indicating nationality
steps.explanation: To indicate your nationality in Romanian you say: Note that in Romanian descriptive words or adjectives — and this includes words showing nationality — change their form to agree with the gender of the person or object they describe. In the dialogue we had the example of Sunt ziaristă (I'm a journalist, agreeing with Rodica). You will find also that, with the feminine gender, there are several different types of ending: Sunt franțuzoaică but Sunt suedeză (I'm Swedish).
steps.callout: Unlike in English, the nationality of a person in Romanian is written with a small initial letter. Capital letters are only used in the names of countries. For example: un englez (an Englishman), englezi (Englishmen), but Anglia (England), Marea Britanie (Great Britain); un american (an American), americani (Americans), Statele Unite (The United States).

steps.title: Asking someone's name and introducing oneself
steps.explanation: To ask someone's name in Romanian we can say either Cum vă numiți? (lit. How do you name yourself?) or Cum vă cheamă? (lit. How do they call you?). In the dialogue we met two ways of presenting oneself: Mă numesc Mike Foster and Eu sunt Rodica Mihai. A third way is to say Mă cheamă Mike Foster / Mă cheamă Rodica Mihai (lit. They call me…). In the phrase Eu sunt Rodica Mihai, eu means 'I'. The persons in Romanian are:
steps.callout: In the dialogue dumneavoastră was used. Unlike English, Romanian has four forms for 'you'. Dumneavoastră (often abbreviated to dvs.) is the most common — this is a polite form. Tu is used to address one person who is a relative or close friend. Dumneata (usually abbreviated to d-ta) is also used to address one person, but when that person is a colleague or subordinate. Voi is used to address two or more persons. Note the different verb forms: Dumneavoastră sunteți englez? — Tu ești ziarist? — Dumneata ești american?

extra_examples.en: What is your name? (lit. How do you name yourself?)
What is your name? (lit. How do they call you?)
My name is Rodica Mihai (lit. They call me Rodica Mihai)

steps.title: The verb a fi (to be)
steps.intro: The infinitive 'to be' is a fi in Romanian. Here are the full present tense forms. Note: the short form e is used in everyday speech instead of este (as in 'E liber aici?' — Is this seat free?).

steps.title: More verbs: a sta, a face, a locui
steps.intro: Two other very common verbs used in the dialogue are a sta ('to stand, to stay, to reside') and a face ('to do'). Another common verb meaning 'to reside, to live' is a locui.

tables.meaning: to stand, to stay, to reside

steps.title: Dialogue 2 — În lift
steps.context: Mike and Rodica meet again in the hotel lift. Rodica asks Mike how to spell his surname.

lines.speaker: Rodica
lines.en: Good evening, what a coincidence!

lines.speaker: Mike
lines.en: Indeed. What floor do you want?

lines.speaker: Rodica
lines.en: The twelfth. And you?

lines.speaker: Mike
lines.en: The ninth.

lines.speaker: Rodica
lines.ro: Scuzați-mă, dar cum se scrie numele dumneavoastră de familie?
lines.en: Excuse me, but how do you spell your surname?

lines.speaker: Mike
lines.ro: Foster. F - o - s - t - e - r.
lines.en: Foster. F - o - s - t - e - r.

lines.speaker: Rodica
lines.en: Thank you. Here is the ninth floor.

lines.speaker: Mike
lines.en: Thank you, goodbye.

lines.speaker: Rodica
lines.en: See you soon, Mike Foster.

steps.title: Spelling names
steps.explanation: From your very first contact with Romania you are likely to be asked to spell your name — on a visa slip when you enter the country, or by a hotel receptionist when you register. The Romanian names of the letters follow the alphabet table. If you want to spell Capital 's' you say se mare; Double 'L' you say doi de le. So 'Seller' would be: Se mare - e - doi de le - e - re.

examples.en: Please write it down for me
How do you spell your name? (lit. How is your name written?)

examples.ro: Cum se spune în limba română…?
examples.en: How do you say in Romanian…? (lit. How is said in Romanian…?)

items.prompt: How do you spell your name?
Where do you live in England?
Where are you staying in Romania?

steps.title: Greetings
steps.explanation: In Dialogue 2 we met the greeting Bună seara ('Good evening'). Here are all the common Romanian greetings. To address someone familiar you simply add the name: Vă rog, domnule Popescu… / Vă rog, doamnă Popescu… / Vă rog, domnișoară Popescu…

steps.title: Numbers 0–100
steps.explanation: From 20 upwards the numbers are followed by de when indicating quantity. Thus: cincisprezece ani (15 years) but douăzeci de ani (20 years). Also note that in colloquial speech the -sprezece ending is clipped to -șpe: unșpe, doișpe, douășpe, treișpe, paișpe, cinșpe, șaișpe, șapteșpe, optșpe, nouășpe. From 21 upwards, numbers follow the pattern: douăzeci și unu, douăzeci și doi… The multiples of ten from 40 to 90 are: patruzeci, cincizeci, șaizeci, șaptezeci, optzeci, nouăzeci.

examples.ro: 21 douăzeci și unu / douăzeci și una

steps.callout: Colloquial clipping: the -sprezece ending becomes -șpe in everyday speech. You will hear this constantly: unșpe (11), doișpe (12), treișpe (13), paișpe (14), cinșpe (15), șaișpe (16), șapteșpe (17), optșpe (18), nouășpe (19).

steps.title: Expressing age
steps.explanation: To ask how old someone is you can say:

examples.en: How old are you? (lit. How many years do you have?)
How old are you? (lit. What age do you have?)

examples.ro: Am douăzeci și doi de ani.

examples.en: I am 15. (no de before ani with numbers under 20)

steps.callout: Note that de is used between the number and the noun only from 20 upwards: cincisprezece ani (15 years, no de) but douăzeci de ani (20 years, with de).

steps.title: Negation
steps.explanation: To give a negative answer to a question or to make a negative statement you use nu before the verb.

examples.ro: Nu, nu sunt englez, sunt american.
examples.en: No, I'm not English, I'm American.

examples.ro: Nu, nu stau la Washington, stau la New York.
examples.en: No, I don't live in Washington, I live in New York.
Are you an Englishman? — Yes, I'm English.

examples.ro: Stați la Washington? — Da, stau la Washington.
examples.en: Do you live in Washington? — Yes, I live in Washington.

steps.callout: Nu is also used when you want to say 'nothing', 'no one' or 'never' using a verb. Romanian uses double negatives — this is correct grammar, not a mistake.

extra_examples.en: I never stay at a hotel.
No one is doing anything. (lit. No one is not doing nothing)

items.prompt: Bună ziua, domnule Andreescu, ce mai faceți?

items.translation: I am staying at the hotel.
